title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

reading.body:
An AI system generated false case citations that a lawyer submitted to a court. The lawyer, representing a client in a civil dispute, included these fabricated cases in a legal brief filed with a county court. The opposing counsel discovered the fake citations during a hearing, revealing that the system had asserted nonexistent legal precedents as real ones.

This is a failure of human review at the point of deployment. The lawyer used an AI tool to assist with legal research and writing but did not verify the citations before filing them in court. A competent check against actual case databases would have caught that the cited cases did not exist. The court ruled that attorneys remain responsible for accuracy regardless of whether they use AI to draft their filings.

It is not established whether the lawyer deliberately used AI knowing it would fabricate citations, or whether he failed to understand the system's limitations. The incident shows one of over 800 documented instances in which AI language models have generated false legal citations when asked for case law.

reports.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed was suspended for submitting a legal brief containing fabricated case citations generated by artificial intelligence. Ahmed, who has practiced law since 2014, represented a food store owner in a civil dispute and cited two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in his filing with Hennepin County Court. The opposing counsel discovered the fake citations during an August hearing, and Ahmed also included false quotations and citation errors in his memorandum.

Judge Lois Conroy ruled against Ahmed's client and ordered payment of $233,563 in back rent. She subsequently fined Ahmed $5,000 and referred him to the state's Professional Responsibility Board. Ahmed agreed to a 30-day suspension of his law license and must pay an additional $900 in costs. Conroy emphasized that attorneys have ethical obligations to provide competent representation and honesty to the court regardless of using AI tools. Over 800 documented instances of AI-generated fake legal citations have been reported.
